newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Manila spurns Beijing claim over smugglers' haven.
newsitem.headline: Manila spurns Beijing claim over smugglers' haven.

text.p: The Philippines on Wednesday flatly rejected China's claim to a cluster of rocks in the South China which serves as a haven for smugglers, saying it has exclusive sovereignty over the area.

President Fidel Ramos publicly repudiated Beijing's ownership of the Scarborough Shoal after an hour-long meeting with Chinese Vice Premier Li Lanqing, which Filipino officials said dwelt solely on increasing economic cooperation.
Li is attending an international business meeting in Manila.
China earlier this month protested against the flying of the Philippine flag on the shoal, calling it a "serious violation" of its sovereignty and demanding the flag's immediate removal.

Philippine fishermen hoisted the flag last month after the navy intercepted a Chinese government radio message instructing one of its ships in the area to raise China's flag on the rocky outcrop, a senior intelligence official said.

The shoal was within the Philippines' exclusive economic zone under the U.N. Convention on the Law of the Sea "and not an area where any other state can exercise sovereign right," Ramos told reporters
"We have the sovereign right to explore and exploit the natural resources of Scarborough Shoal and to undertake other activities in that area," he added.

Located on the high seas 200 km (125 miles) west of Subic freeport near Manila, the shoal is a 16-km (10-mile) long rock formation which almost entirely vanishes at high tide, except for an outcrop big enough to accomodate just 12 people.
With an unclear economic value, the rock appears an odd prize for a contest between an Asian giant sitting on a huge land mass and a neighbour with more than 7,000 islands of its own.
Military officials say the shoal has served in recent years mainly as a transit point for small boats carrying smugglers and their contraband to the Philippines' main island of Luzon.
The row over the shoal erupted a few days after Manila protested against an alleged incursion by Chinese naval ships into areas it claims in the Spratly Islands well south of Scarborough.
Beijing, which insists all islands in the South China Sea historically belong to China, said the ships were scientific vessels on a research mission.
The Spratlys are also claimed wholly or in part by Vietnam, the Philippines, Taiwan, Malaysia and Brunei.
"There is no dispute there (Scarborough Shoal) in regard to sovereignty," Ramos told his weekly news conference, adding, "Scarborough is not within the disputed Spratly Islands."

"With respect to the South China Sea as a whole ... the Philippines stands ready to continue bilateral and multilateral dialogues aimed at reaching a negotiated settlement of all disputes," Ramos added.
